1.  Which gene is the transcriptional “master” (i.e. acts upstream)?  
   •  Knocking out G2 alone abolishes all resistance (0 %).  
   •  Any double mutant that carries g2 (g1g2, g2g3) is also 0 %.  
   •  Therefore the absence of G2 masks the state of the other genes; G2 must lie upstream and is epistatic to the others – exactly what is expected for a transcription factor that turns the pathway on.  
   ⇒  G2 is the transcription factor.

2.  How do G1 and G3 relate to one another?  
   •  g1 retains 75 % resistance, g3 50 %.  
   •  When both are removed (g1g3) resistance collapses to 10 %, far below either single mutant.  
   •  Thus each can supply (part of) the resistance when the other is missing, but neither alone gives full wild-type activity; they therefore behave as partially redundant genes.

3.  Which way does epistasis run between G1 and G3?  
   •  In the g1 g3 double the phenotype is far more similar to g1 ( strongly reduced compared with g1 but still far below g3’s 50 %), so G1’s absence dominates over G3’s; i.e. G1 is epistatic to G3.

Putting these points together matches only one of the offered statements:

(D) G2 is a transcription factor, G1 and G3 show gene redundancy, G1 is epistatic towards G3

Answer: D
